summary: A document camera crossed with an AIY-style voice kit. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W sits in a small head pod with a Camera Module 3 Wide looking down at the page, two I2S MEMS microphones and a MAX98357A I2S amp (the Google AIY Voice HAT v1 audio design, built from breakouts). The head hangs from a 15 in hollow lamp gooseneck that leaves the base pointing up and turns down into the head's top; only a 10-wire ribbon runs through it (power up, speaker and two signals down). A two-part printed base holds the 40 mm speaker, the talk button, an 8-LED status bar, the USB-C input and 425 g of bought steel discs clamped to the arm's threaded pipe. A DPDT toggle on the head cuts the microphones' data line and supply. A printed shutter covers the lens. No custom PCB.
architecture: Power: Raspberry Pi 15 W USB-C supply (5.1 V, 3 A) -> USB-C breakout in the base (5.1 k CC resistors) -> 120 mm of 22 AWG to the base junction protoboard -> 3 x 5 V + 3 x GND conductors up the arm -> the bonnet's 5 V rail, pins 2/4 (back-powering the Pi through the header)
Base 5 V also feeds: NeoPixel stick through a 1N4001 diode (drops VDD to about 4.3 V so 3.3 V data is a valid high), and the talk button's green LED through 220 ohm
Compute: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W with header, in the head, on a Perma-Proto Bonnet Mini that carries all head wiring

Camera: Camera Module 3 Wide (IMX708, 102 x 67 deg) -> 38 mm Standard-Mini FPC (15-pin 1 mm to 22-pin 0.5 mm, from the official Zero case kit) -> Zero 2 W CSI connector; sensor's long side along the page's long side; fixed lens position set on the first unit
I2S bus (Pi is master, googlevoicehat-soundcard overlay, 48 kHz): BCLK GPIO18 (pin 12), LRCLK GPIO19 (pin 35), DIN GPIO20 (pin 38) from the mics, DOUT GPIO21 (pin 40) to the amp
Mics: 2 x SPH0645 breakouts share BCLK/LRCLK (through 1 k series resistors) and one DOUT line; left mic SEL to GND, right mic SEL to the switched mic supply

Amp: MAX98357A breakout in the head, VIN from 5 V, SD_MODE on GPIO16 (pin 36, as on the AIY Voice HAT), which selects the left channel, so the client plays mono; software caps it at 2.5 W; speaker pair runs down the arm to the 40 mm 4 ohm speaker in the base

Mute (hardware): DPDT toggle on the head. Pole 1: COM = Pi 3V3, throw A = mic VDD, throw B = red LED + GPIO24 (pin 18) sense. Pole 2: COM = GPIO20, throw A = mic DOUT, throw B = GND. Muted = the mic data line open and GPIO20 grounded (this is what makes it real), and the mic supply disconnected (left floating)

Camera-on light: green LED + two 220 ohm in parallel (about 10 mA) on GPIO25 (pin 22), lit by software whenever the camera is streaming (software only, by choice); the printed lens shutter in the head is the hardware camera-off
Status light: NeoPixel stick (8 x 5050) in the base on SPI0 MOSI GPIO10 (pin 19) with core_freq=250, data wire down the arm to 440 ohm (2 x 220) at DIN; SPI keeps it off the I2S pins
Talk button: 16 mm momentary on the base top, GPIO23 (pin 16, AIY convention) to GND with internal pull-up, debounced in software, wire down the arm
Arm harness (10 x 28 AWG silicone ribbon, 690 mm): 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED data, 9 GND, 10 BTN; runs through head nipple, coupling, gooseneck, coupling, base nipple

Mechanical stack at the arm root: coupling in a seat on a 2 mm collar on the base top -> 1-3/4 in 1/8 IPS nipple, 8 mm into the coupling, down through the top shell, a printed column and two 3 in steel discs -> hex nut under the discs, discs on 8 mm floor ribs; the pipe end stays 3.9 mm above the harness groove floor so the wires can turn out

params.radioModule: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W on-board 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 4.2 (Raspberry Pi states modular compliance certification)
params.firstArticleNote: order A builds 2 units to measure (assembly step 1); order B buys the rest and the spares
params.pipeThreadOdNote: NPS 1/8 pipe OD is 0.405 in (10.29 mm, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nominal_Pipe_Size); no lamp-part seller publishes the thread major diameter, so measure a nipple on the first unit
params.armMassNote: estimate: 0.84 g/mm, from a 300 mm gooseneck that weighs 252 g (QTX 188.293UK), times 381 mm; Grand Brass publishes no weight
params.armBendNote: estimates (Grand Brass publishes neither); measure them on the first gooseneck
params.armOuterDiameterNote: estimate, used only to draw the figure (no check or CAD part reads it): Grand Brass publishes no outside diameter, so the figure draws the gooseneck between the 10.29 mm thread and the 15.9 mm coupling; measure the first gooseneck
params.figEstimatesNote: estimates, used to draw the figure and by cad/_system.py to size the bought parts in the whole-product check (no engineer check or printed part reads them): board, connector and package sizes from typical parts and the boards' drawings, where the BOM gives none. Sizes are mm. A box is length x width x height, a round part diameter x height, a nut across flats x thickness and an axial part length x diameter. Positions on the Pi run along it from its SD end and across it from its port edge
params.coreFreqNote: rpi_ws281x README: on a Pi 3 (the Zero 2 W has the same BCM2710A1) set core_freq=250 or the SPI clock has the wrong frequency for the NeoPixels
params.inputConnectorRatingNote: 3 A is what USB-C receptacles are built for; Adafruit gives no current rating for the 4090 breakout, only that its 5.1 k CC resistors ask the source for up to 1.5 A by default
params.ampEfficiencyNote: estimate: the datasheet gives 92 % only for 8 ohm at 1 W; efficiency into 4 ohm is lower
params.cameraLensPositionNote: start value: 1 / 0.28 m, the middle of the 220 to 345 mm lens-to-page range; set it on the first unit with the test page
params.harnessWireOrder: 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED data, 9 GND, 10 BTN (a ground between the speaker pair and the LED data wire, and between LED data and BTN)
params.cadNote: CAD numbers below. Head parts are drawn in the head frame: origin at the head centre in plan, z = 0 on the head's bottom face, x along the head, +y toward the child; the 15 deg tilt is applied at assembly. Base parts use the base frame (origin at the base centre on the desk).
params.grilleNote: the PUI AS04004PR-R spec sheet gives a 35.6 mm baffle opening; at a 3.2 mm pitch the 97 holes span 35.3 mm

assembly: First article. Order A (order-a.csv) buys parts for 2 units. Build both with these steps, then check every item below and write what you measure into design.json; rerun `sprue cad ponder` and `sprue all ponder`, and place order B (order-b.csv) only when every item passes. Gooseneck: hollow, male 1/8 IPS thread at both ends, mass (320 g assumed), the rigid threaded length at each end (12.7 mm assumed) and the tightest bend it holds (40 mm radius assumed). Bore: the 10-wire harness pulls through the gooseneck and both nipples by hand (it needs about 6 mm). Nipple thread OD (10.29 mm assumed): it passes the 11 mm arm holes without forcing. Base stack: with the nipple 8 mm into the coupling and the nut tight, its lower end is at least 3.4 mm above the groove floor and the gooseneck still gets 5 mm or more of thread in that coupling. Head: the camera's holes sit on the four pins, the lens clears the closed shutter, the 38 mm cable reaches both connectors without strain, the toggle body (13.2 x 13.2 mm assumed) clears the camera with the head closed, the SD card goes in and out, the mic sound holes are centred on the ports, and the M2.5 screws clamp the Pi without bottoming. Base: the junction board drops onto its posts, the USB-C socket is centred in the back-wall opening, the speaker (18.3 mm tall) sits in its ring, and the feet fit their 8.4 x 2 mm pockets. Inserts: an M3 screw tightened into an insert in a 4.0 mm hole does not spin it. Kits: the bonnet kit's 2x20 header is female (it must press onto the Pi's male header) and the Seeed Basic Kit contents are listed; if the kit includes an SD card or a supply, drop that line from order B. Electrical, from the test sheet (step 34): 5 V at the bonnet stays at 4.75 V or more, the USB-C meter reads 2.6 A or less, and `vcgencmd get_throttled` reads 0x0. Wi-Fi: with the head closed, `iw dev wlan0 link` reads no more than about 10 dB below a bare Zero 2 W in the same spot. Mechanical: the drop and tip tests in step 35 pass.

Tools: soldering iron with a fine tip plus M3 and M2.5 heat-set insert tips; multimeter with a continuity beeper; USB-C power meter; digital calipers; a 1 g kitchen scale; drill bits or pin gauges from 5 to 8 mm to gauge the bore; flush cutters; wire strippers for 22 to 28 AWG; Phillips #0 and #1 screwdrivers; a 5/8 in wrench for the nuts; soft-jaw pliers or a strap wrench for the round couplings; a deburring tool for the nipple ends; a 0.5 mm steel pull wire or fish tape at least 500 mm long; tweezers; a PCB holder; a set square; a luggage scale for the tip test; a hot-glue gun; a heat gun; a computer with Raspberry Pi Imager and a microSD reader.

Consumables for 20 units (not in the order list or the total): lead-free solder 0.5 to 0.8 mm (about 50 g) and a flux pen; hot-glue sticks (about 20); medium-strength threadlocker such as Loctite 243 (10 ml); polyimide (Kapton) tape 12 to 20 mm wide (1 roll); heat-shrink assortment 1.5 to 6 mm; 1 mm double-sided foam tape (1 roll); paper tape for tape flags; a white paint marker; isopropyl alcohol.

Before building, ask the school's IT staff: is there a 2.4 GHz network the Pi can join (the Zero 2 W has no 5 GHz), is it WPA2-Personal or WPA2-Enterprise, must devices be registered by MAC address, and can the Ponder backend host be allowlisted. The unit test sheet needs the answer.

Golden SD card, step 1 of 4. In Raspberry Pi Imager pick Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W and Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). In the settings set hostname ponder-00, a user, your SSH key and Wi-Fi country US, and the school network if it is WPA2-Personal. Write and verify, then edit config.txt on the card's boot partition: add `dtoverlay=googlevoicehat-soundcard`, `dtparam=spi=on` and `core_freq=250` (the Zero 2 W has the Pi 3's SoC, whose SPI clock follows the core clock and would upset the NeoPixel timing), and comment out `dtparam=audio=on` so the voice card is the only sound card.

Golden SD card, step 2 of 4. Boot it in the first unit's Pi (or any Zero 2 W) and run `sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y sox python3-picamera2 python3-venv rpicam-apps-lite`, then make a venv at /opt/ponder/venv and `pip install adafruit-circuitpython-neopixel-spi` in it. Find the voice card's name with `aplay -l`. Write /etc/asound.conf so the default device is that card by name, played through a softvol control with `max_dB -1.1` (caps the amp at 2.5 W of its 3.2 W) and recorded straight from the card. If the school uses WPA2-Enterprise, add the network now with `nmcli` (802-1x settings from IT).

Golden SD card, step 3 of 4: keep frames and audio off the card. Turn off any swap file or partition on the SD card (`swapon --show` may list zram only), set `Storage=volatile` in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, and make /tmp a tmpfs (`findmnt /tmp` shows tmpfs). The overlay file system goes on per unit, last (step 33).

Golden SD card, step 4 of 4: the client. The Ponder device client is not written yet (the B0tes/ponder-tutor repo holds the web app only). When it exists, install it from a tagged release into /opt/ponder as a systemd service that reads the backend URL and a per-unit token from /etc/ponder/device.conf. It must: debounce GPIO23 (push-to-talk) in software, read mute from GPIO24, turn on GPIO25 before it starts the camera and off after it stops, drive the light bar on SPI at no more than 50 % brightness, play mono (the amp plays the left channel only), hold the camera at a fixed lens position (3.6 dioptres to start, set on the first unit), never use a Bluetooth headset's microphone (the hardware mute covers the built-in mics only), and keep frames and audio in RAM. Then shut down, copy the card to an image file with Imager or `dd`, and write that image to all 21 cards. Label each card with a unit number.

Check the prints. Base top, base bottom, head upper, head lower and shutter are PA12 (MJF, grey as printed); the diffuser is natural PETG. Clear loose powder out of holes and slots. The shutter should slide its full 18 mm in the head lower's track with its thumb nub through the floor slot.
Press in the heat-set inserts with the iron at about 220 C, square and flush: 6 x M3 in the base top bosses, 4 x M3 in the head upper bosses, 4 x M2.5 in the head lower's Pi posts.

Harness: cut 690 mm of the 10-wire ribbon. It is all black, so count from one edge and put a numbered tape flag on wire 1 and wire 10 at both ends, and a HEAD flag on one end. Order: 1-3 5V, 4 GND, 5 SPK+, 6 SPK-, 7 GND, 8 LED data, 9 GND, 10 BTN. Beep every wire end to end with the meter. Peel the wires apart along the middle, keeping 30 mm joined at each end so the order stays and the bundle goes round through the pipe.

Bonnet: solder the 2x20 header that comes with the Perma Proto Bonnet Mini onto it. All head wiring goes on the bonnet. Signal jumpers are single wires peeled from the rest of the two ribbons, cut 120 mm so the shells can lie side by side, with a tape flag naming each end. Use 22 AWG from the hook-up set for the amp's VIN and GND, in two colours kept the same on every unit.

Mics: put a 1 k resistor in the BCLK line from GPIO18 (pin 12) and one in the LRCLK line from GPIO19 (pin 35); both mics share these two lines after the resistors. Each mic's GND goes to GND. Join both mics' 3V pins into one wire (mic VDD) and both DOUT pins into another (mic DATA); both go to the toggle. Tie the left mic's SEL to GND and the right mic's SEL to mic VDD.

Mute toggle: pole 1 COM to 3V3, throw A to mic VDD, throw B to GPIO24 (pin 18) and, through 220 ohm, to the red LED's anode; red LED cathode to GND. Pole 2 COM to GPIO20 (pin 38), throw A to mic DATA, throw B to GND. Sleeve every lug in heat-shrink. With the meter, find the lever position that joins COM to throw B: that is MUTE.

Amp: VIN to 5V and GND to GND (22 AWG), BCLK to GPIO18 and LRC to GPIO19 (straight from the Pi pins, not through the 1 k resistors), DIN to GPIO21 (pin 40), SD to GPIO16 (pin 36). Leave its terminal block off; the speaker pair solders to its + and - pads later. Camera light: GPIO25 (pin 22) through two 220 ohm in parallel to the green LED's anode, cathode to GND. Heat-shrink the LED legs and in-line resistors.

Head upper, before the arm goes on: push the green LED into the front hole nearer the camera end and the red LED into the other one, from inside, and fix them with hot glue. Mount the toggle in the end-wall hole with its nut so the lever points down at the engraved MUTE in the MUTE position. Seat each mic in its pocket with its sound hole over the shell's port, and run hot glue round the board edge without covering the port.

Arm: deburr the inside of both nipple ends. Mark the 1-3/4 in nipple 8 mm from one end with the paint marker. Screw the 1/2 in nipple through the head upper's top hole with a nut inside and a coupling outside, and tighten. Screw the gooseneck into that coupling, the second coupling onto its lower end, and the marked end of the 1-3/4 in nipple into the second coupling up to the mark. A drop of threadlocker on every thread. Before it sets, turn the head so its long side is parallel to the base's front edge when the arm is in the pose of step 32 (check against a square).

Pull the harness through with the pull wire: BASE end in from inside the head upper, through the head nipple, the gooseneck and out of the bottom of the 1-3/4 in nipple. Leave 130 mm inside the head and the rest out of the bottom. Slide a 25 mm piece of 6 mm heat-shrink over the bundle where it will leave the base nipple, and shrink it.

Solder the harness HEAD end to the bonnet: wires 1-3 to the 5V rail (pins 2 and 4), wires 4, 7 and 9 to GND, 5 and 6 (SPK+, SPK-) to the amp's speaker pads, 8 (LED) to GPIO10 (pin 19), 10 (BTN) to GPIO23 (pin 16).
Head lower: drop the shutter into the camera end of its track (the end without lips), thumb nub down through the floor slot, and slide it over the window. It has to go in before the camera.

Camera: plug the wide (15-pin) end of the 38 mm Standard-Mini cable into the camera, contacts toward the camera board. Seat the camera lens-down on the four pins with the cable edge toward the Pi end, and hold it with a small dab of hot glue on each of the four pins. Check the shutter still slides under it.

Pi: push the SD card in first (it can't go in once the Pi is mounted, because the end wall is 2.5 mm away). Plug the narrow (22-pin) end of the camera cable into the Pi's camera connector, contacts toward the board, and close the latch. Screw the Pi to the four M2.5 inserts with M2.5 x 6 screws, SD end toward the end away from the camera. The cable makes one short loop between the two connectors; don't crease it.

Base top, upside down: fit the talk button through its hole with the ring nut inside. Press the speaker into the ring under the grille, cone toward the grille, and run hot glue round its rim. Glue the diffuser into the light-bar slot from inside (flange against the top skin), lay the NeoPixel stick in its frame behind it with the LEDs toward the diffuser, and run hot glue along both long edges of the stick onto the frame rails so it can't drop when the base is turned over.

Arm root: from the outside, push the 1-3/4 in nipple through the base top's arm hole and column until the coupling sits in its seat on the collar. Cover the top face of one steel disc with Kapton, leaving the centre hole clear. Thread the harness tail through that disc (Kapton face toward the shell), then the second disc, then a nut, and let them hang on the wires for now.

Junction board (quarter Perma-Proto): bring in USB-C VBUS and GND from the breakout on 120 mm of 22 AWG each (the two power colours), with a strain-relief loop at the breakout, and the harness's 5V (1-3) and GND (4, 7, 9). From 5V, the 1N4001 (stripe toward the stick) to the stick's 5V, and 220 ohm to the talk button's LED anode. GND to the stick's GND, the button LED's cathode and one button leg. Harness LED wire (8) through two 220 ohm in series to the stick's DIN, as close to the stick as the wire allows; BTN (10) to the other button leg; SPK+ and SPK- (5, 6) to the speaker. Trim every lead flush on the solder side and cover that side with Kapton.

Press the junction board onto its two posts and heat-stake the pins: touch each pin tip with the flat of the iron until it mushrooms over the hole. Then slide the discs and the nut up the wires onto the nipple and run the nut up tight with the wrench, so coupling, shell, column and discs clamp together; hold the gooseneck with the strap wrench so it doesn't twist. The Kapton face of the top disc now sits about 2.8 mm under the board's Kapton-covered solder side.

Set the USB-C breakout in the cradle on the bottom plate with its socket in the back-wall opening and fix it with hot glue on the cradle walls, so plugging in can't move it. Lay the harness tail in the groove under the nipple and out through the gap in the disc ring.

Before first power, with the bonnet unplugged from the Pi and no supply connected, beep with the meter: harness 5V to GND at the bonnet is not a short (the reading climbs as the capacitors charge); the BTN and LED wires show no continuity to 5V; BTN shows continuity to GND only while the talk button is held; bonnet 3V3 to GND is not a short. Fix anything that fails before going on.

First power, bonnet still off the Pi: plug in the 15 W supply through the USB-C meter. At the bonnet's header, pins 2 and 4 read 4.9 to 5.1 V, the LED and BTN pins read under 1 V, and the 3V3 pins read 0 V. Unplug, press the bonnet onto the Pi's header, and stick the amp flat on top of the bonnet over the middle of the Pi with a square of 1 mm foam tape.

Close the head: bring the lower shell up under the upper so the lip seats all round with no wire across it, then drive 4 x M3 x 8 up through the wells in the lower shell into the inserts. Check the shutter nub still slides.

Close the base: fit the bottom plate with 6 x M3 x 8 up through its counterbored holes, with no wire under the lip. Stick the four rubber feet into their pockets. Write the unit number in the engraved UNIT NO. field with the paint marker.

Pose: hold the base down on the desk with one hand and bend the gooseneck with the other (the unit tips at about 1 to 2 N at the head otherwise) to the design pose: lens 220 mm above the desk and 120 mm in front of the arm root, head nose-down about 15 deg, long side parallel to the base's front edge.

Per-unit software: boot, then set the hostname to ponder-NN (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_hostname ponder-NN`), write the backend URL and this unit's token into /etc/ponder/device.conf, record the Wi-Fi MAC (`cat /sys/class/net/wlan0/address`) for IT, turn on the overlay file system (`sudo raspi-config nonint do_overlayfs 0`) and reboot.

Unit test sheet (every unit; write each result in the build log). Load: run a 10 minute soak with the camera streaming (`rpicam-vid -t 600000 --nopreview -o /dev/null`), a tone through the speaker (`speaker-test -c 2 -t sine -f 440`) and the light bar white; every minute read `vcgencmd measure_temp` and `vcgencmd get_throttled`, and measure 5V at the bonnet with the meter. Pass: under 80 C, get_throttled 0x0 at the end, 5V at 4.75 V or more (if it dips, lower the volume or brightness cap). Light bar: a sweep script lights each of the 8 pixels red, green, blue and white in turn, at idle and during the soak. Page: put a Letter test page with pencil text in all four corners and the middle in front of the base, open the shutter, take `rpicam-still --lens-position 3.6 -o test.jpg`, copy it off with `scp`, and read every corner at full resolution. Closed shutter: the image is black. Mics: record 5 s of stereo while talking (`arecord -c 2 -r 48000 -f S32_LE -d 5 t.wav`), then compare `sox t.wav -n remix 1 stat` and `remix 2 stat`: both channels carry the voice, within about 6 dB. Speak at a normal voice from 60 cm and check it is clearly heard on playback. On MUTE: the red light is on, both channels are silent, and GPIO24 reads high (`pinctrl get 24`). Speaker: at the volume cap a spoken prompt is clear from 60 cm. Lights and button: `pinctrl set 25 op dh` lights the green light; after `pinctrl set 23 ip pu`, `pinctrl get 23` reads lo while the talk button is held. Wi-Fi: `iw dev wlan0 link` shows the school network with the head closed.

First article only, after its test sheet passes: tip test, pressing down on the head and pushing it sideways at head height with a luggage scale (the checks say it tips at about 3.7 N down and 1.2 to 2.4 N at head height; record what it takes). Drop test: drop the unit from desk height (760 mm) onto the head, then onto a base corner, then run the test sheet again. Record any crack, loose part or failed test, and fix the design before order B.

Close the shutter, put the unit in its box with its supply (use only the supplied adapter, as the base says), and record the unit number, SD card, Wi-Fi MAC, test results and date in the build log. Tell the teacher to hold the base when moving the arm.
costNotes: Import duty on the Raspberry Pi kits. Seeed ships them from China under DAP terms, so the carrier collects US duty before delivery. Seeed's customs page cites a 45% base tariff on dev boards: about $207 on the $459.90 of kits if it applies.

Tariffs Mouser may add. A reviewer read 'a tariff of 8% may be applied if shipping to the United States' on the Camera Module 3 Wide page (about $56 on $700); Mouser pages would not load here, so this and the other Mouser lines are not confirmed. Mouser's shipping insurance (about $7.20 on $875) is extra too.

The print prices ($1,349.41 at Craftcloud) come from an unverified rate of $0.30/cm3 with a $6 minimum a part, not a quote. Upload the six STLs to Craftcloud's quote tool (PA12 MJF and PETG) before ordering.

Shipping is an estimate for every shop except LightingSupply.com and SparkFun over $100, and the lead days are the shops' own; the Seeed order also needs DHL transit (2 to 5 working days) and customs. Jameco adds a $5 fee to orders under $10, which order A is.
Consumables and tools (assembly steps 2 and 3), sales tax, and the second round of shipping if you order in two phases (see Order in two phases, under Build).
estimates: armMassG 320: 0.84 g/mm from a 300 mm gooseneck that weighs 252 g (QTX 188.293UK), times 381 mm, because Grand Brass publishes no weight. Both tip checks use it, so weigh the first gooseneck.
armMinBendRadiusMm 40 and armEndRigidMm 12.7: Grand Brass publishes neither. The arm-reach check uses both, so measure them on the first gooseneck.
armOuterDiameterMm 12.7: Grand Brass publishes no outside diameter, so the figure draws the gooseneck between the 10.29 mm thread and the 15.9 mm coupling. Only the figure uses it.
pipeThreadOdMm 10.29: the NPS 1/8 pipe OD (0.405 in, Wikipedia's Nominal Pipe Size table). No lamp-part seller publishes the thread's major diameter, so measure a nipple on the first unit.
cameraMa 250: an allowance, because Raspberry Pi publishes no current figure for the Camera Module 3. The power check uses it.
ampEfficiencyPct 85: the MAX98357A datasheet gives 92 % only for 8 ohm at 1 W, and efficiency into 4 ohm is lower. The power check uses it.
cameraLensPositionDioptres 3.6: a start value, 1 / 0.28 m, the middle of the 220 to 345 mm lens-to-page range. Set it on the first unit with the test page.

The fig* params: board, connector and package sizes from typical parts and the boards' drawings, where the BOM gives none. The figure and the whole-product check (cad/_system.py) use them (figEstimatesNote says how each size is written); the check's clearance findings beside an estimated size (the SD card, the LED flange, the Pi's radio) need the part measured.

cad/_system.py's own estimates: the masses of the parts no seller weighs (about 35 g in all, each marked in system.json), the light cones (a 5050 RGB LED about 120 deg, a diffused 5 mm LED about +/-30 deg) and the share of the light bar that gets out (70%, from the drawing, as no source gives one). Only the whole-product check uses them: weigh the parts and look at the light on the first unit.
